name: Command palette
markup: No html in this file. Each variant below carries the path to its own markup at r/command-palette/<variant>.html — fetch the one you need.
description: A ⌘K overlay for jumping to a record or firing an action by typing. It is a shortcut over the navigation, never the only route to something.
when_to_use: Consoles a person lives in all day with many destinations and records. Skip it on a three-page app — nobody will learn the shortcut.
rules: Everything reachable here must also be reachable by clicking. The palette is an accelerator, not a hiding place.
Both ⌘K and Ctrl-K must work, and both need .prevent — the browser binds ⌘K to the address bar.
x-cloak on the overlay, otherwise it paints over the page on first load.

A palette is a combobox, not a menu, because it has a text box. A menu moves real focus between its items; a combobox keeps real focus in the input and points at the active row with aria-activedescendant. So the rows are not buttons and not links: nothing inside role="option" may be focusable, and a row that is a tab stop puts the caret outside the search box the moment somebody presses Tab.

Because a row cannot be a link, the palette has no middle-click, no open-in-a-new-tab and no status bar saying where the row goes. The handler navigates, and a handler is not a link — which is one more reason every destination in here has to exist as a real anchor on a real page. Ship the palette as the only route to a screen and that screen cannot be bookmarked, opened in a second tab, or reached by anybody who does not know it is there.

The palette is a dialog as well as a combobox. It covers the page with a dimmed overlay, so it takes role="dialog", aria-modal="true" and a name, and it has to hold focus to earn them: aria-modal on a panel Tab can walk out of tells a screen reader the page behind is inert while the keyboard proves it is not. The two go in together or neither does.

x-trap.noscroll on the overlay does the focusing, the returning and the scroll lock, so show() sets three fields and focuses nothing itself. The trap opens on [autofocus], which is why the query input carries one: without it the trap lands on the first tabbable node, which is the Esc button. Do not also focus by hand. x-show has not written display when $nextTick runs, so focus() on the input is a silent no-op, and a bare requestAnimationFrame beats Alpine's flush, so a hand-rolled call would be racing the trap for the same element and losing on its own terms.

The row id is derived from the record — :id="'cp-' + o.id" — never from the loop index, because filtering renumbers the rows and aria-activedescendant then names whichever record moved into that slot. Key the loop on the same field or Alpine reuses nodes and the id and the row drift apart. The prefix belongs to the palette, so a second one on the page needs a second prefix or both write the same ids.

Closing returns focus to whatever opened the palette, which is not always the trigger — ⌘K fires from wherever the caret already was. x-trap captures document.activeElement when it activates and puts it back on close, so this needs no bookkeeping of its own. Without that, every dismissal drops a keyboard user at the top of the document.
The letters on the action rows are the application's own shortcuts, shown so people learn them. The palette does not listen for them, and must not: inside a search box, N types an N.

What the palette shows at rest is not the catalogue with no filter applied. Every open starts on the empty query, so that state is where the palette spends most of its life, and 1,284 orders in recency order is a list nobody reads and a first keystroke that looks like a reset. It is a short set somebody chose: the last few records this person opened and the handful of actions their role fires. The first of them is already highlighted, because ⌘K then Enter to reopen what you were last in is the single most common thing anybody does with a palette.

Where results are ranked into one list rather than split into groups by kind, the kind has to ride on each row as a word. PO-24-1187, GRN-1187 and VEN-1187 are three records to three different screens, and an icon is not enough to separate them: a 16px document glyph is the same glyph for an order and an invoice, and it is not an accessible name either.

Ranking sorts, and a sort needs a tiebreak that is not the score. Rows scoring the same have to keep the order they were in, or two keystrokes that match equally well swap the rows under the pointer and Enter takes a record nobody chose.

A row this account may not fire keeps its place in the list, greyed, with the reason under it. aria-disabled announces and blocks nothing, so the arrow keys have to step over it, the pointer must not highlight it, and the click handler has to return early. Hiding it instead means somebody searches for the same thing again next week, and it makes the list a different shape for every role.
The reason a row is unavailable is grey, not red. Red says a record is overdue or a request failed; an approval limit that has always applied is neither.

An action that needs an argument opens a second step rather than firing. The row says so by ending in an ellipsis, choosing it clears the query and puts a chip in the box naming what was already chosen, and Backspace on an empty query goes back a step — as does the first Escape, which is why Escape here pops rather than closes until there is nothing left to pop.

A prefix character narrows the palette to one kind — > actions, # records, @ people — and only at position 0, so a query with a hash in the middle of it is still a search for that text. The character stays in the box as typed text rather than being lifted into state, so there is one source of truth for the mode and Backspace is what leaves it. The prefix alone, with nothing after it, lists the whole of that kind: that is how anybody finds out what the mode holds.

Records are searched on the server; actions are not. Filtering a dozen strings the template already holds does not need a round trip, and an action list that arrives late is an action list that is missing at the moment somebody types three letters and presses Enter. So the two halves of the list come from two places, and the keyboard reads the rows out of the DOM rather than out of an array, because htmx replaced half of them without telling Alpine.

One highlight mechanism, not two. Where part of the list is swapped in by htmx, the tint is painted by one function over whatever role="option" elements are in the DOM — the Alpine-rendered rows included. A :class binding on the Alpine half and classList on the server half is two implementations of one state, and they drift apart on the first keystroke that lands mid-request.

Below sm there is no ⌘K, no Escape key and no pointer. The trigger has to be a real button, the way out has to be a control inside the panel, and the overlay has to be a column anchored to the top edge — a centred panel opens exactly where the software keyboard is about to be.

The palette is included once, by the shell. Two copies on one page is two ⌘K handlers racing, two overlays, two focus traps and two sets of row ids, and the second set silently wins every getElementById the first one does.

An action that changes something is a POST. A palette row that navigates to a GET which mutates is fired by anything that follows links — a prefetcher, a preview, somebody restoring their tabs — so the row submits a hidden form carrying the CSRF token instead.

anatomy.description: A dimmed field with the panel near the top, not centred — the list grows downward. It carries x-trap.noscroll, so it is what holds focus and locks the page behind.
role="combobox", focused on open and holding real focus the whole time the palette is up. The query is cleared on close so the next open starts fresh.
Results split by kind — actions, records — each under a small label. role="group" named by that label, and a group with no matches leaves with its heading.
One row, role="option" and not a tab stop, with the active one tinted. The keyboard drives which is active.
The word on a row saying what sort of record it is — order, receipt, vendor, item. It rides on the row wherever the results are one ranked list, because there is no heading above the row to say it.

What sits in the box on the second step of an action that needs one more thing. It names what was already chosen, is aria-hidden because the input's own label and the listbox name carry it, and Backspace on an empty query is what removes it.
What the list shows at zero matches — the query quoted back, not an empty panel.
What the empty state offers instead of a dead end: the searches the palette cannot run itself, drawn as ordinary role="option" rows so Enter still leads somewhere.
A sr-only role="status" inside the dialog, carrying the number of matches. It sits inside because aria-modal hides everything outside the dialog from a screen reader.
The key legend. Nobody learns arrow keys and Enter from nothing — and where the palette has prefix modes, this is where they are written down.

behaviour: Everything reachable here is also reachable by clicking. The palette is an accelerator, never a hiding place.
Both Cmd-K and Ctrl-K open it, and both need .prevent — the browser binds Cmd-K to the address bar.
Opening moves focus into the query input, and Tab stays inside the panel, so nothing behind the overlay is reachable until it closes.

An empty query shows the last records this person opened and the actions their role uses, not the unfiltered catalogue, and the first row is already highlighted so ⌘K then Enter reopens the last record.
Typing filters both groups at once, and every keystroke puts the highlight back on the first match, so Enter always takes the row at the top of the list.
Where the results are one ranked list rather than groups, every row says which kind of record it is, because the same number is an order, a receipt and a vendor code.

Arrow down and up move the active row over the flattened list in the order the rows are drawn, not group by group, and clamp at both ends rather than wrapping. Enter takes the active row, Escape closes.
The highlight follows the mouse as well as the keyboard, so the row under the pointer and the row Enter would take are never two different rows.
A row this account may not fire stays in the list with the reason under it, and neither the keyboard nor the pointer will put the highlight on it.
A group whose rows are all filtered out goes with its heading, and when nothing matches at all the list is replaced by an empty state naming the query.
Nothing matched leaves rows behind rather than an empty panel: the searches the palette cannot run itself are offered as options, so Enter always leads somewhere.

A row whose label ends in an ellipsis asks for something before it fires. Choosing it clears the query, puts a chip in the box naming what was chosen, and shows the second list. Backspace on an empty query goes back one step, and so does the first Escape.

A first character of >, # or @ narrows the palette to actions, records or people. The character stays in the box, so deleting it is what leaves the mode, and the character on its own lists the whole of that kind.

Records are searched on the server on a debounced query with a two-character floor, while the actions are matched in the browser. Below the floor the record rows are cleared, so last search's answer never sits under a query that did not produce it.

Below sm the overlay is the screen: no scrim, the box at the top edge where the keyboard cannot cover it, the list scrolling in what is left, and a Cancel control in the panel because there is no Escape key to press.
Closing clears the query, so reopening does not present the previous search as if it were current, and puts focus back on whatever opened the palette.
On a three-page application, skip it entirely — nobody will learn the shortcut.
accessibility: The input is role="combobox" with aria-autocomplete="list", aria-expanded, aria-controls naming the list and aria-activedescendant naming the active row.

The list is role="listbox" with an accessible name and every row is role="option". No row carries aria-selected: a palette commits nothing — a row is fired and the palette closes — so the only state a row has is being the active one, and aria-activedescendant is what carries that.
Real focus never leaves the input. The highlight moves through aria-activedescendant, which is why every row needs a stable id derived from the record and why no row is a tab stop.

A row is never an anchor or a button. Nothing inside role="option" may be focusable, so the row is a div and the navigation happens in the handler — which is a real cost, and the reason the same destination has to be a real link somewhere else.

Each group is role="group" named by its heading, and the visible heading is aria-hidden — the group is already named, and a bare paragraph is not a permitted child of a listbox. A container that is only there to be a swap target takes role="none", which drops it out of the tree and leaves its options exposed to the group above.

A disabled row keeps aria-disabled="true" and keeps its place. aria-disabled is an announcement and not a behaviour: the arrow keys, the pointer and the click handler each have to honour it separately.

The number of matches is announced from a role="status" inside the dialog. Outside it the announcement would never arrive, because aria-modal="true" takes everything outside the dialog out of the accessibility tree.

When the palette changes step or mode, the input's accessible name and the listbox name change with it and the status says which step it is on. The chip drawn in the box is aria-hidden, because those two already carry it and a third copy is read out as loose text beside the field.
The overlay is role="dialog" with aria-modal="true", named "Command palette", so the rest of the page is out of the accessibility tree while it is open.
The trigger carries aria-haspopup="dialog", and any ⌘K hint drawn inside it is aria-hidden — it is a reminder of the shortcut, not part of the button's name.
Focus is trapped in the panel and cannot reach the page behind. The trap opens on the query input because it carries autofocus, rather than on the Esc button, which is the first tabbable node.

Escape closes and returns focus to whatever opened the palette, captured by x-trap at the moment it activated. Where the palette has steps, the first Escape pops the step and only the last one closes.
